explanation: Birds walk on their toes, so the joint you see is the ankle, bending the same way ours does. The real knee is tucked up close to the body, hidden by feathers.

claims.text: The joint halfway down a bird's visible leg that seems to bend backwards is its ankle.
That joint is neither the bird's knee nor its hip.
A bird's ankle bends in the same direction as a human ankle.
A bird's knee sits close to its body and is usually hidden by feathers.

Confident players may report it, which is why the explanation spells out the reasoning.

evidence.restatement: The joint halfway down a bird's leg that appears to bend backwards is the intertarsal joint between the tibiotarsus and the tarsometatarsus, which is the bird's ankle.

evidence.restatement: The visible joint is neither the knee, which sits higher and close to the body, nor the hip.
Birds are digitigrade: they stand and walk on their toes, with the heel held off the ground.
A bird's ankle flexes in the same direction as a human ankle; it only looks reversed because the heel is raised.
A bird's knee lies close against the body and is normally covered by feathers.
The joint that appears to bend backwards in the visible part of a bird's leg is the ankle, between the shin bone and the long foot bone.
Since that joint is the ankle, it is neither the knee nor the hip.
Birds stand and walk on their toes; the long bone below the ankle belongs to the foot.
A bird's ankle flexes the same way a human ankle does, with the heel end pointing backwards.
The bird's knee sits high against the body and is normally covered by body feathers.
